Stripped
STRIPT
v. (past part.)
From Old English strypan, to plunder, to despoil. Webster 1828: pulled or torn off; deprived; made naked; robbed. The Authorized Version also keeps the older form stript. Scripture uses it of Joseph, of Job, of the man on the Jericho road, and of Christ before the soldiers.

Biblical Definition

Stripped in Scripture marks the moment a man is reduced to nothing, and the same word runs from Genesis to the passion. Joseph’s brothers begin with the coat: when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him (Genesis 37:23) — the token of the father’s love removed before the pit and the sale. Job uses it of God’s dealing with him: He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head (Job 19:9), and it is three verses before I know that my redeemer liveth. Our Lord’s parable puts it on the Jericho road: a certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead (Luke 10:30) — and the priest and the Levite pass a man who has nothing left to identify him. Then the word reaches its end at the Praetorium: they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe (Matthew 27:28), and afterward they took the robe off and led Him away to be crucified. He who stripped Himself of the form of God was stripped by soldiers, and the garments were parted and gambled for at the foot of the cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STRIP as to pull or tear off, as a covering; to deprive of a covering; to make naked; to deprive; to divest; to rob or plunder. All the senses are violent, and Scripture’s uses are all involuntary.

expand to see more

STRIP, v.t. — To pull or tear off, as a covering; to deprive of a covering; to make naked.

To deprive; to divest; to bereave; as, to strip a man of his possessions or his honors.

To rob; to plunder; to pillage; as, robbers strip a house.

STRIPPED, STRIPT, pp. — Deprived; made bare; plundered.

The Authorized Version uses both spellings; stript at Genesis 37:23 and stripped at Luke 10:30 and Matthew 27:28.

Key Scripture

Genesis 37:23 — "And it came to pass, when Joseph was come unto his brethren, that they stript Joseph out of his coat, his coat of many colours that was on him;"

Job 19:9 — "He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head."

Luke 10:30 — "And Jesus answering said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him of his raiment, and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead."

Matthew 27:28 — "And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe."

Philippians 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture never sentimentalizes the stripping of a man, and that the God who permits it is the God who was stripped Himself.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What deserves recovery is Job 19:9 and its position. He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head — Job says it of God, not of the Sabeans or the Chaldeans, and Scripture never corrects him for it. He had already said, the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD, and the book’s narrator says he sinned not nor charged God foolishly. The comfort available to a stripped believer is not that God had nothing to do with it. It is that God had everything to do with it and is nevertheless his Redeemer, which is precisely what Job says three verses later, standing in the ashes with nothing left.

The Jericho road and the Praetorium belong together. In the parable the stripped man is passed by a priest and a Levite, and the neighbour turns out to be the despised Samaritan — a story our Lord told in answer to a lawyer looking for a boundary on the command to love. In Matthew 27 the stripped man is Christ Himself, mocked with a scarlet robe and a reed and a crown of thorns, and the passers-by wagged their heads. Philippians 2 says He had already stripped Himself before any soldier touched Him: made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. Nothing was taken from Him that He had not first laid down, and that is the difference between His stripping and every other in Scripture.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pashat (H6584), to strip off, to flay, to make a raid; Greek ekduo (G1562), to strip off clothing; kenoo (G2758), to empty, in Philippians 2:7.

expand to see more

Hebrew pashat (H6584) — to strip off, to flay, and also to make a raid; Genesis 37:23, 1 Samuel 19:24.

Greek ekduo (G1562) — to take off, to strip; Matthew 27:28, 31, and Luke 10:30.

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty, to make void; made himself of no reputation (Philippians 2:7).

Hebrew ketoneth passim — the coat of many colours, or of long sleeves, stripped from Joseph.

Greek himation (G2440) — an outer garment; the raiment parted among the soldiers at the cross (Matthew 27:35).

Usage

"They stript Joseph out of his coat (Genesis 37:23) — the token of a father’s love taken first."

"He hath stripped me of my glory (Job 19:9) — a sufferer naming God as the agent and still calling Him Redeemer."

"They stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe (Matthew 27:28) — the last stripping, and a willing one."
